Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The Most Gracious. Taught the Qur'an. Created man. Taught him the explanation (al-bayan). The sun...﴾

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat al-Rahman

It is Meccan according to the majority of scholars, and some of them said it is Madinan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Gracious﴾. Al-Hasan said: it is a name that no one can claim for himself. It is also said: it is a name that cannot be shared. It is not correct to say it of anyone other than Allah, whereas it is correct to say "raahim" and "raheem" of others, because the meaning of al-Rahman is that His mercy encompasses everything, and this does not apply to anyone other than Allah, the Majestic and Exalted. Some of them related that al-Rahman is the combination of the opening letters of three surahs: "Alif-Lam-Ra", "Ha-Mim", and "Nun".
"And His saying ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, meaning: He made it easy and facilitated its learning."

Verse 3 of Surah al-Rahman: "He created man (al-insan)."

And His saying "He created man (al-insan)." Qatadah said: it is Adam, may the blessings of Allah be upon him. Al-Dahhak said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). And from some of them: it is the human species, a singular used in the sense of the plural, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds...﴾, meaning, the people.

And His saying ﴿He taught him the bayan (clear expression)﴾. According to the view we mentioned, that the intended one is Adam, the meaning of teaching the bayan is teaching the names. According to the view that says it is Muhammad (ﷺ), the meaning of teaching the bayan is that He made clear to him the lawful and the unlawful. It is also said: He made clear to him the path of guidance and the path of misguidance. And it is said: He made clear to him good and evil. And if we take it to refer to the genus of mankind, then the meaning of bayan is speech and articulation, and every discerning intelligent person has a bayan by which he understands and distinguishes.

And His saying, ﴿The sun and the moon [run] by a reckoning﴾, meaning by a calculation. This was said by Mujahid and others. It is also said that "bi-husban" means by a known course through known stations. Al-Suddi said: by a known term, so when they reach their appointed term, they perish. It has also been said that al-hisban is the pivot of the millstone, and the meaning is that they revolve as the millstone revolves on its pivot.

Wa qawluhu: ﴿wal-najmu wash-shajaru yasjudan﴾ (“And the star and the tree prostrate”). The people of lexicography (ahl al-lughah) said: al-najm is everything that grows without a stalk (saq), and ash-shajar is that which grows upon a stalk. It is also said: al-najm is the star of the sky, and ash-shajar is all trees.

As for their prostration, Ibn ʿAbbas said: they prostrate when the sun rises and while the sun declines until it sets. It is also said: their prostration is what God, exalted is He, has subjected them to by His will and command. The more preferable view is to say: the prostration of inanimate things is established by the explicit text of the Book, it is as God, exalted is He, intended, and knowledge of its reality is entrusted to Him; this is the position of the People of the Sunnah. It is also said: their prostration is by the turning of the shadow to the right and to the left.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 7:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And the sky He raised high﴾ mean: He elevated it to such a height that hands cannot reach it.

And His words: ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first is that it refers to the well-known balance (scale). The second is that what is meant by it is justice.

And His saying: ﴿That you not transgress in the balance﴾. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "lā taṭghaw fī al-mīzān" (that you not transgress in the balance), meaning: do not act unjustly in it, and do not exceed the limit. Ṭughyān (transgression) is going beyond the limit.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 9:

And His saying: ﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾, meaning: with fairness (ʿadl). And establishing the weight is: setting the tongue of the balance straight, without inclination or injustice.

And His saying: ﴿And do not make deficient the balance﴾, meaning: do not diminish and do not defraud. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "O assembly of the mawali (meaning: the non-Arabs, the ʿajam), you have been put in charge of two matters through which many nations before you were destroyed: the measure (al-mikyal) and the balance (al-mizan)."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 10:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And the earth — He laid it out for all creatures﴾. That is: He spread it out. Regarding al-Anam (all creatures) there are three opinions. The first, reported by al-Hasan al-Basri, is that it refers to jinn and humankind. The second is that it refers to humankind alone. The third is that it refers to everything that crawls and moves.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Therein is fruit﴾. Al-fakiha (fruit) is everything one enjoys eating (yatafakkahu bihi).

And His saying: ﴿and palms with sheaths﴾. Al-akmam is the plural of kumm (sheath, covering), and kumm is everything that covers something. From this comes the well-known kumm (sleeve), so called because it covers the hand. The qalansuwa (cap) is called kumma, because it covers the head. The meaning of kumm here is: the husk (ghilaf) that surrounds the fruit of the date palm. It is also said: the kumm is the tal' (spathe, the sheath enclosing the palm flower cluster).

The Exalted said: ﴿And the grain, with its husk, and the fragrant plant.﴾ Al-'Asf: the leaves of the crop; when it dries it becomes chaff (tibn). It is also said that al-'asf is the herbage that grows out of the earth.

And His saying: ﴿wa-r-rayḥān﴾ (and the fragrant plant), meaning: the fruit. Ibn Kaysan said: when the crop grows, its beginning is 'asf, then al-rayḥān appears in it, and it is its fruit. It has also been said that al-rayḥān is sustenance (al-rizq). The poet said:

(Peace from God and His rayḥān... and His mercy and a cloud of pearls)

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: it is the rayḥān that is smelled. The most preferred of the opinions is that al-'asf is the chaff, and al-rayḥān is the grain in which there is food for eating; it was named rayḥān because from it comes the sustenance of the servants. In the codices (al-maṣāḥif) it reads: "wa-l-ḥabb wa-l-'asf," and its meaning: and He created the grain possessing husk.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 13:

And His saying: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ Its meaning: By which of the blessings of your Lord do you two deny, O humankind and jinn? The intended meaning of "ālā' (favours) is the blessings which He enumerated earlier. It has been established, by the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir from Jabir, that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited Surat al-Rahman to his Companions, but they did not respond with anything. So he said: "What is wrong with you, that I see you silent? The jinn were better than you in responding. Every time I recited to them this verse, ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾, they said: 'Nor do we deny any of Your blessings, our Lord, and to You belongs all praise.'"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 14:

The words of God Most High: ﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾. Ṣalṣāl (dry clay) is dry earth that makes a sound when it is struck and shaken.

And His words ﴿like pottery﴾ mean: al-khazaf (fired earthenware).

If it is said: He said elsewhere, ﴿from clay that sticks﴾ (ṭīn lāzib), and He said elsewhere, ﴿from black mud altered⁠—﴾ (ḥama masnūn), and here He said ﴿from ṣalṣāl﴾. So what is the way to reconcile these?

The answer: all of them are true, without doubt. God Most High created Adam from dust, made it into clay that sticks, then made it into altered black mud, then made it into ṣalṣāl like pottery, then formed him. Qatadah said: it is the water that reaches the earth, then the water departs, and the place where the water was dries, hardens and cracks, and this is the ṣalṣāl like pottery. Abu al-Husayn ibn Faris mentioned in his tafsir that it has been related in some hadith that when God Most High willed to create Adam, peace be upon him, He made the dust into clay that sticks and left it for forty years, then made it into ṣalṣāl like pottery and left it for forty years, then formed it and left it as a body without a soul in it for forty years. The angels would pass by it and say: "Glory be to the One who created you for a purpose."

It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that Iblis, may he be cursed, when he saw the form and found it hollow, knew that it was a creature that could not hold itself together.

The Lord's words, the Exalted: ﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾, meaning: from the flame of fire. It is also said: from the pure essence of fire. And the jinn is the father of the jinn.

And His saying: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ — we have already explained its meaning. Al-Hasan said: "The jinn is Iblis."

And His saying: ﴿from a smokeless fire﴾ — we have already mentioned it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The marij is the greenness that appears between the fire and the smoke." It is also said: "The marij is a fire mixed with blackness." Al-Farra' said regarding His saying ﴿from fire﴾: "It is a fire beyond the veil, and from it are the thunderbolts that people see."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 17–18:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ means: the rising-point of summer and the rising-point of winter. As for the one who said in another place: ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾, it is the rising-point of each day in summer and winter. And it is said: the two easts are the sun and the dawn (al-fajr), and the two wests are the sun and the twilight (al-shafaq).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 19:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting each other﴾. That is: He let them loose and sent them forth. This is what al-Farra' (al-Farra'), al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) and others said. It is also reported from some of them: "Maraja al-bahrayn" means "laqiya baynahuma" (he made them meet between them).

As for His words ﴿the two seas﴾, there are several opinions. Mujahid (Mujahid) said: the sea of the sky and the earth. al-Hasan (al-Hasan) said: the sea of Persia (Fars) and the Romans (al-Rum). It is also said: the sea of the East and the sea of the West. And it is said: the salt sea and the sweet sea.

As for His words ﴿meeting each other﴾, that is: one of them reaches the other.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 55, verses 20–21:

And His saying: ﴿Between them is a barrier; they do not transgress.﴾ That is, its barrier. And His saying: "they do not transgress," meaning: neither of them mixes with the other. The salt does not mix with the sweet [so as to spoil it], nor the sweet with the salt so that it becomes brackish. It is also said: the barrier is a barrier of power.

The verse was revealed concerning a specific place in the sea of Persia (Fars) and the Roman sea. It is also said: concerning a specific place where the sweet and the salt meet. The sweet water is the Nile, and the salt water is the Roman Sea; they meet but do not mix.

Some of them said: the barrier is the land between the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. And it was related from some of them that the barrier is the Arabian Peninsula.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 22–23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From both of them come forth the pearls and the coral﴾. It is also read "yakhruju" (with a different vowelling) and "yukhraju" (in the passive), meaning: Allah brings them forth. As for al-lu'lu' (pearls), it is the well-known gem, both small and large. As for al-marjan (coral), Ibn Mas'ud said: it is a red bead. It is also said that it is [al-basad], a well-known jewel. Qatadah and others said: al-marjan is the large pearls and al-lu'lu' is the small ones. It was also said the reverse: al-marjan is the small pearls and al-lu'lu' is the large ones.

If it is said: He has said ﴿from both of them﴾, and the scholars of this matter agree that it comes forth from the salt water and not the sweet water. The answer: He mentioned both, while meaning only one of them, as the Arabs say: "I ate bread and milk," whereas eating was only in one of them and not the other. Al-Zajjaj said: When He mentioned the two seas and then mentioned the pearls and the coral, which come forth from only one of them, the attribution to both was used in the manner of the Arabic language. Al-Qaffal al-Shashi mentioned in his tafsir that the pearls and coral only occur at the meeting point of the two seas at the beginning of their creation; then the place of the shells is the salt sea and not the sweet sea. So the saying ﴿from both of them﴾ is correct, because they are at the beginning at the meeting point of the two seas. This is a good view if it is so.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when the sky rains, the shells rise to the surface of the sea and open their mouths, and whatever drop of rain falls into their mouths becomes a pearl.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 24–25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And His are the ships, the lofty ones [al-munsha'at] that raise up [their sails]﴾. It is also read with a kasra on the shin (al-munshi'at), but the first (reading, with fath) is more well-known. The meaning of the word with fath is "the raised up" (al-marfu'at) in construction (al-shar', i.e., the sails or the masts), and it is said: "the created things" (al-makhluqat). The meaning of the word with kasra is "the ones that cause to rest at noon" (al-muqilat), and it is said: "the ones that begin the voyage" (al-mubtada'at fi al-sayr). Upon this meaning, when it is read with fath, its meaning is: I begin with them in the journey. This was related by al-Azhari (al-Azhari). Al-jawari (the running ones) are the ships.

And His saying: ﴿in the sea like landmarks﴾, that is, the mountains. The poet said: (When they cut across a landmark, a landmark appeared...)

And al-Khansa' said:

(Indeed Sakhr, the guides take their guidance from him... as if he were a fire-marker upon his head)

That is, a mountain. It is also said: "like landmarks," that is, like palaces. And it is related from some of them that the ships on the sea are like the mountains on the land.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away.﴾ That is: everyone upon the earth is perishing.

And His Face will remain: meaning, your Lord will remain. Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that what is meant is that what is intended by "the Face of your Lord" will remain.

"Full of Majesty and Honour" (dhu al-jalal wa al-ikram): meaning, the Greatness and the Magnificence. As for al-ikram (Honour), it is that He honours His friends and chosen servants.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 29–30:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾. There are several opinions regarding this verse. The first: whoever is in the heavens asks Him for mercy, and whoever is on the earth asks Him for provision and forgiveness. Al-Kalbi said: none among the people of the heavens and the people of the earth is independent of Him. Qatadah said: the people of the heavens and the people of the earth ask Him for forgiveness. It is related from some of them: whoever is in the heavens, namely the angels, asks for forgiveness and provision for the people of the earth, and whoever is on the earth asks for forgiveness and provision for themselves. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. Thus, the one being asked in both questions is the people of the earth. The summary is that the meaning of the verse is: all the people of the heavens and the people of the earth ask Him for their needs, and none is independent of Him.

And His words: ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾. Abu al-Darda' related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises a people, and lowers others."

It is related from some of them: He gives to the one who asks, answers the one who calls, and frees the captive. It is related from some of them: He gives life and causes death, honors and humbles, creates and provides. It is related from some of them: He frees necks, gives to the needy, and silences the eloquent speaker.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 31–32:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two weighty ones﴾, that is: the jinn and mankind.

The word thaqal (weighty one) in the speech of the Arabs refers to everything that is coveted and desired. They call the eggs of the ostrich thaqal, because people compete for them. And in the report it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have left among you the two weighty things (al-thaqalayn): the Book of Allah and my family (ʿitrah)." This is an indication of the great rank of both.

If it is said: He says "We will soon attend to you (sanafrugh)", and freedom from concern (faragh) occurs only after preoccupation, and preoccupation is not permissible for Allah, the Exalted, so how is its meaning [to be understood]?

The answer: This is in the manner of threat and warning, like a person who says to another: "I will attend to you," while he is not at that moment preoccupied with anything. Al-Zajjaj said: Faragh (attending/freeing oneself) occurs in two senses. The first: freedom from occupation. The second: in the sense of intention (qasd), like a man who says to another: "I have now turned myself to your harm and hurting of me" (tafarraghtu li-adhaya wa-makrihi), meaning: I have begun upon my harm and hurting. And a man says to another: "Wait until I attend to you (atafarragh laka)," meaning: I will target you and make you my aim. So the meaning of His saying ﴿We will soon attend to you﴾ is: We will intend and aim at you with reckoning and recompense.

Al-Mubarrad recited in this sense the verse of Jarir:

(When the Iraqi smith feared for his backside... I turned myself toward the slave bound in fetters)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 33–34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾. That is, the sides of the heavens and the earth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 46–47:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾. When He mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers, He followed it with mention of the bliss of the believers.

On the authority of ʿAṭiyya ibn Qays: "The verse was revealed concerning the man who instructed his sons, saying: 'When I die, burn me, grind me up, and scatter me in the wind, for perhaps I will be able to elude Allah.' Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) drank some milk, then asked about it, and it had come from a source other than he knew, so he vomited it up, and Allah revealed this verse.

And His saying: ﴿two gardens﴾, that is, orchard (bustān). It is also said: a bustān for his dwelling and a bustān for his servants and retinue. It is also said: a residence for him and a bustān for him. And on the authority of some of them, its meaning is: the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss, and this is a good opinion. Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 54–55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿reclining on couches whose linings are of brocade﴾. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Its linings" means its outer surfaces. The Arabs say: "This is the inner side of the sky (batn al-sama'), and this is its outer side (zahr)," in reference to what is seen of the sky. This view was also mentioned by al-Farra'. As for the rest of the exegetes, they said: the intended meaning of "linings" is literally the lining (bitana).

Al-Istabraq (brocade) is thick silk brocade, like what is hung of brocade on the Ka'ba. It was also said: it is a Persian word arabized from their saying istabr. It is reported from some of them that it is like Chinese silk.

Abu Hurayra said: "These are the linings; so what do you suppose the outer surfaces to be?" A similar report is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Its outer surfaces are a light that shines." It is reported from some of them: its outer surfaces are of what Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿So no soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes﴾.

His saying: ﴿and the fruit of the two gardens is near at hand﴾, meaning the fruits of the two gardens are within easy reach. From this is the saying of the Arabs: "This is my fruit-picking, good are its dates," since every picker brings his hand to his mouth. It is narrated concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when he entered the treasury (bayt al-mal) in Kufa and saw the gold and silver in it, that he said: "O yellow one, and O white one, deceive someone other than me!" Then he said: "This is my picking..." to its end.

His saying: ﴿near at hand﴾ means easy to reach. Qatada said: "Neither thorn nor distance keeps it away." Others said: one can reach it standing, sitting, and lying down.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 56–57:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿In them are those restraining their gaze, whom neither man nor jinn has touched before them﴾. If it is said: how does He say ﴿in them﴾ (fihim) when He has only mentioned the two gardens?

The answer: Some of them said: the two are mentioned with a plural form, so it is permissible for the discourse to refer back to the two with a plural form. The more correct view is that His statement ﴿in them﴾ (fihinna) refers to the couches (furush), and its meaning is "upon them" (alayhinna), like His statement ﴿and I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾, meaning: upon the trunks.

His statement ﴿restraining their gaze﴾ means: they have restricted their glances to their husbands, not seeing anyone else. This is the best of the qualities of women. Ibn Mas'ud said: they are not displaying their adornment (mutabarrijat), nor are they loud-voiced (dammakhat), nor are they foul-smelling (dafirat). Some of them said: they are not sulky (mutashArrighat), nor peering (mutatalli'at), nor shrieking (sayyahat), nor clamorous (sakhkhabat). Al-Hasan said: they are not those who wander about the markets.

His statement ﴿whom neither man nor jinn has touched before them﴾ means: no human or jinn has had intercourse with them. Al-Farra' said: al-tamth is intercourse accompanied by the shedding of blood, which is deflowering (al-iftidad).

Al-Farazdaq said:
(They have been raised to me, untouched before me, / and they are purer than ostrich eggs.)

It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that the intended meaning of His statement ﴿In them are those restraining their gaze﴾ is the believing women among humans. On this basis, some said: it is permissible for a jinn to have intercourse with a human woman, and they took evidence from the apparent meaning of the verse. However, most scholars rejected this and said: the meaning of the verse is: no jinn has touched them, the jinn woman being a jinn, and no human man has touched the human woman being a human. His statement ﴿In them are those restraining their gaze﴾ encompasses both human and jinn women. If someone says: do they say that jinn enter Paradise and have spouses like humans?

The answer: The scholars differed on this. Some said: God admits the believing jinn into Paradise just as He admits the disbelieving jinn into the Fire, and this is the view of Damrah ibn Jundub and others. Others said: they have no reward. Layth ibn Abi Sulaym said: believing jinn will be protected from the Fire and then they will be made into dust, while the disbelieving among them will abide forever in the Fire.

As for the first view, if we take the verse to refer to the dark-eyed houris (al-hur al-'in), none of these questions arise.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 62–63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And below them are two gardens﴾, meaning: below the two gardens are two (other) gardens. It is said: the two gardens mentioned first are for those brought near (al-muqarrabun), and the two mentioned last are for the people of the right (ashab al-yamin). It is also said: the two mentioned first are for the foremost (al-sabiqun), and the two mentioned last are for the followers (al-tabi'un).

Scholars differed concerning His saying: ﴿And below them are two gardens﴾. Some of them said its meaning is that the two gardens mentioned last are below the two gardens mentioned first in bliss and honour. Others said: it is derived from "dunuw" (nearness) in the sense of proximity, as if these two gardens are closer to the believer, meaning: to his dwelling and abode, than the first two gardens. If someone says: what honour is there in mentioning two gardens, when here only one garden is mentioned?

The answer: moving from one orchard to another carries a degree of delight and pleasure that is not hidden, so the mention of two gardens is for increase, honour and blessing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 68–69:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Therein are fruit, and date-palms, and pomegranates.﴾ It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The pomegranate is not among the fruits, and likewise the ripe date (rutab), because they were singled out for mention apart from the fruits. al-Farra' also mentioned this. But this report from Ibn 'Abbas is a strange opinion (qawl gharib), and most scholars hold that all of them are fruit, because fruit (fakiha) is that which one enjoys (yatafakkahu bihi), and singling them out for mention is to draw attention to a particular kind of excellence, not that they are not among the fruits. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Guard over the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾, and like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il [...]﴾.

The pomegranate is a kind of fruit that is sucked (yumassu) and whose pulp (thafl) is spat out. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: If a man said to his wife, "If you eat fruit, then you are divorced," and she ate a pomegranate or a ripe date, the divorce takes effect. This is the view of most scholars and it is the preferred opinion (al-mukhtar). According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, the divorce does not take effect.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The palm trees of Paradise have trunks of gold, their sheaths of gold, their spathes (karanif) of emerald, their fronds (sa'af) are the clothing of the people of Paradise, and their fruit is like buckets, sweeter than everything and softer than everything.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 72–73:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Fair ones, restrained in their pavilions﴾. That is: confined (maḥbūsāt). It has also been said: these pavilions are outside Paradise, like the deserts relative to the settled towns."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 76–77:

The Most High's words: ﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾. Al-Farra' said: "It means the gardens of Paradise." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The carpets of Paradise." It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾, that it means: a green rafraf (rafraf) which filled the horizon, and it is the carpet (basat). In general: the rafraf is any spread that is raised, derived from the raff (raff), which is the raised part of a wall.

His words: ﴿and beautiful green carpets﴾. It was read in the irregular reading: "'abaqari hisan" (abaqari hisan). Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "'Abqari hisan" (abqari hisan) means the cushions.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the tanafis (tanafis, rugs of fine fabric). It is reported from some of them: the zara'i (zara'i, the finest carpets). And 'abqari (abqari) is a village in Yemen where embroidered fabric (al-washy) is woven, and they attribute to it everything fine. In the book "Kitab al-Gharibayn" it is stated that 'Abqar is a village inhabited by the jinn, and the Arabs attribute to it everything superior. The poet said:

(A miserly people over it, a jinn-like garden of 'abqar, deserving of one day attaining and rising above.)

Some have mentioned that 'abqari here means embroidered fabric (al-washy). Mujahid said: it is brocade (al-dibaj). It is reported from some of them: it is brocade worked with gold. As for the report narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said about 'Umar: "I did not see an 'abqari who makes his work (fariyah) like him," its meaning is: I did not see a leader and distinguished man of a people performing his deed.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾. It is also read: "Dhī al-Jalāl wa al-Ikrām" (Possessor of Majesty and Honour, in the genitive). Its meaning: Possessor of greatness and awe. It is also said: "Dhū al-Jalāl wa al-Ikrām" means He magnifies the believers and honours them. The first opinion is more preferable, because it refers to the greatness of God and the exaltedness of His station.

His saying ﴿Dhū al-Jalāl﴾ (in the nominative) refers to the Name, and His saying ﴿Dhī al-Jalāl﴾ (in the genitive) refers to the Lord. The Name and the named are one according to most of the People of the Sunnah. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Cling to saying, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour" (alladhū al-jalāl wa al-ikrām), meaning: persist in it and keep at it.

If someone says: What is the meaning of the repetition of His saying ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you both deny?﴾ in this surah? It would have been enough to pause on the meaning with one occurrence.

The answer: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, according to what they were accustomed to and recognised in their speech. It is among their customs that when they mention blessings bestowed upon a person, they repeat the reminder to be grateful, or the mention of reproach for ingratitude. God, exalted is He, enumerated the blessings in this surah and mentioned this phrase after every blessing, so that they would not forget to be thankful for them, would recognise God's beneficence towards them, and would renew praise for them. End of the surah.
